title: Barista Express or Pro: what to upgrade, if anything

questions.text: Which machine do you own now?
What bothers you most about it?
options: Shots: fast, sour, thin or different every time
The grind, dose, tamp and steam routine itself
Weak steam, shots that only drip, or coffee not hot enough
Nothing specific, it just feels old

questions.text: How many milk drinks do you usually make in a row?
Have you tried fresh beans (5–20 days after the roast date) with a full dose and a firm tamp?
options: Yes, and the shots still disappoint

descale.title: Descale before you decide anything
descale.text: Weak steam, shots that only drip and coffee that isn't hot enough are all listed as descale symptoms in the manufacturer's own troubleshooting table. Run a full descale, then answer again. No source gives a lifespan for these machines, so these symptoms alone don't prove yours is worn out.

keep.title: Keep it and change nothing
keep.text: If the shots taste good and the steaming doesn't bother you, a new machine won't fix anything. Run the cleaning and descale cycles when the machine asks for them, buy beans with a roast date, and keep your money.

beans-test.title: Run the fresh-beans test first
beans-test.text: The manufacturer lists a coarse grind, too small a dose and a light tamp as the causes of fast shots, and says stale beans run fast too. Buy beans with a 'Roasted On' date, use them 5–20 days after roasting, dose so the tamper cap sits level with the rim, then pull three shots in a row. You can also adjust shot temperature on both machines.

grinder.title: Keep the machine, add a standalone grinder
grinder.text: If fresh beans and a proper dose still give fast, sour or inconsistent shots, the built-in grinder is your bottleneck. A standalone espresso grinder is the cheapest real fix, and it isn't wasted if you move later: the Dual Boiler has no grinder, so you'd need one anyway. Don't buy 54 mm extras if a machine change is likely.

steam-single.title: Keep it: the wait matters most for back-to-back drinks
steam-single.text: A dual boiler's main gain is steaming while it brews, which pays off when you make several milk drinks in a row. For one drink at a time, keep your machine. If the steam has got weaker than it used to be, descale first.

dual-boiler.title: Dual Boiler, plus a standalone grinder
dual-boiler.text: If you make several milk drinks in a row and the wait to steam after each shot is what annoys you, a dual boiler brews and steams at the same time. It has no built-in grinder, so budget for one, and it takes a 58 mm portafilter, so your 54 mm accessories won't carry over. Owner reliability reports are mixed. Barista Pro owners have a weaker case here, since the Pro heats quickly.

oracle-jet.title: Oracle Jet, if you want less work
oracle-jet.text: It grinds, doses and tamps for you and textures milk hands-free. It heats with a ThermoJet, not boilers, so don't count on it steaming while it brews. Owners of the original Oracle called its built-in grinder 'a bit meh' on back-to-back drinks, so automation may not settle the grinder question.

oracle-dual-boiler.title: Oracle Dual Boiler, for less work and several milk drinks
oracle-dual-boiler.text: It automates grind, dose, tamp and milk, and its dual boilers let it steam while it brews, which helps with several drinks in a row. Owners of the original Oracle praised the workflow but some found the grinder coarser on back-to-back shots and kept an external grinder. Your 54 mm accessories won't fit its 58 mm portafilter.
